newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Fears linger in the shattered streets of Grozny.
newsitem.headline: Fears linger in the shattered streets of Grozny.

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov, who emerged as probable winner of Chechen elections on Tuesday, offers a bright future of independence to his people, but in the ruins of the shattered capital doubts and fears linger.
Picking their way through streets lined with the charred hulks of buildings left by 21 months of battles with Russian troops, they need no reminder of their troubled past.
Certainly, many believe Maskhadov can win the peace as he won the war.

But signs of tension between different elements of Maskhadov's victorious guerrilla army were evident in the comments of some fighters who had voted for his main rival, youthful and hardline field commander Shamil Basayev.

"I want Maskhadov to be our president. I think he will look after us and do all he can for us," said one middle-aged woman on her way to Grozny's open-air bazaar, virtually the only shopping available since most of the city centre was flattened.
"Look what Yeltsin did to us," cried one elderly ethnic Russian woman, recalling her sufferings during the war. Her priority was to get her pension. Moscow had not been paying it.

"I think that today Maskhadov is the best man to stabilise the situation in Chechnya," one smartly dressed young man said, saying he did not want to see a strict Islamic republic of the kind proposed by Basayev and others.
"They (the Russians) will have to recognise us now, we're people too, like Portugal or Holland. We're not monkeys -- see, we can talk," said another.
Further down the street, a couple of Chechnya's ubiquitous camouflage-clad irregular armed guards said they had voted for Basayev. But they were not too concerned that he had lost.
"What's the difference? They're all good," one said, laughing.
But other Basayev voters were less happy.
"If Maskhadov becomes president, there will be no stability in the republic," one middle-aged man said.
"Although he's a soldier, he's weak. The people who voted for Maskhadov are opposed to independence."

Another Grozny man, hunching against the bitter winter cold that has settled over the Caucasus, complained that Maskhadov would not be as tough with Moscow as Dzhokhar Dudayev, the charismatic chief who declared unilateral independence in 1991.
"To deal with Russia, we ought to have somebody tougher, like Dudayev," he said. Dudayev was killed in a rocket attack last April.

Maskhadov, who negotiated the peace deal with Moscow that culminated in Monday's presidential and parliamentary elections, is seen as more open to compromise by the Kremlin, although he also insists on winning full sovereignty.
Asked what Russia's reaction to the election would be, Chechens seemed unconcerned.
"What Russia thinks is of no interest to us. It's a separate republic, not our territory," said one armed fighter.
"Yeltsin's done all he can to us," said another, civilian, Grozny resident, surveying his ruined city. "What Yeltsin wants makes no difference to us now."
